title: Design: Insert, Delete, GetRandom in O(1)
oneLiner: A set with O(1) insert, remove and uniform random pick. A list gives random access, a map from value to index gives fast lookup, and swap-with-last makes removal O(1).
keyTakeaway: Keep the values in a list (random pick = one random index) and a dictionary from value to its index in that list (O(1) membership). To remove, move the LAST value into the removed value's slot, update its index in the map, and pop the end. No shifting, so every operation is O(1) on average.
explanation:
Design a class RandomizedSet with Insert(val), which adds val and returns true if it was not already present; Remove(val), which removes it and returns true if it was present; and GetRandom(), which returns a uniformly random current element (it is only called when the set is non-empty). All three must run in O(1) on average.

The grader runs a list of operations. For insert and remove it checks the returned booleans. For getRandom it calls your method 300 times and checks that every value returned is currently in the set and that every current element came up at least once, which a uniform pick does with overwhelming probability and a biased or stale one does not.

No single built-in structure does all three. A hash set has O(1) insert and remove but cannot pick a random element without walking it. A list can pick list[random index] in O(1), but finding and removing a value is O(n). So use both: a List<int> of values and a Dictionary<int, int> from value to its index in the list.

Insert: if the value is in the map, return false. Otherwise record index[val] = list.Count and append it. Remove: if it is not in the map, return false. Otherwise look up its index i, take the last value of the list, write it into slot i and set index[last] = i, then remove the list's last slot and delete val from the map. Order within the list doesn't matter, which is the whole trick: removing from the end is O(1), removing from the middle is not. GetRandom: list[rng.Next(list.Count)].

Every operation is O(1) on average (hash map operations plus O(1) list work), and the two structures together use O(n) space. The same "swap with last, then pop" move deletes from any unordered array in O(1).

The visualization runs insert 10, 20, 30, then remove 10: the array is the list and the map shows value to index.

visualizationSteps.message: values is a list (random pick by index); indexOf maps each value to its slot (O(1) lookup).
Insert 10: it goes at the end, slot 0, and indexOf[10] = 0.
Insert 20: it goes at the end, slot 1, and indexOf[20] = 1.
Insert 30: it goes at the end, slot 2, and indexOf[30] = 2.
GetRandom: pick a random slot from 0 to 2. Each value is equally likely.
Remove 10, at slot 0. Don't shift: copy the last value, 30, into slot 0 and set indexOf[30] = 0.
Pop the end and delete 10 from the map. The list is out of order, which never mattered, and every step was O(1).

pythonHarnessPreamble:
def run_randomized_set(ops, args):
    # insert and remove report their booleans; getRandom is called 300 times and reports
    # whether every pick was a current member and every member was picked at least once.
    s = RandomizedSet()
    shadow = set()
    results = []
    for op, a in zip(ops, args):
        if op == "insert":
            results.append(s.insert(a[0]))
            shadow.add(a[0])
        elif op == "remove":
            results.append(s.remove(a[0]))
            shadow.discard(a[0])
        else:
            picks = [s.get_random() for _ in range(300)]
            results.append(all(p in shadow for p in picks) and set(picks) == shadow)
    return results
recognitionSignals: O(1) insert, delete AND random access, or delete from an array whose order doesn't matter.
"Design" questions where one structure handles lookup and another handles position.
gotchas: Forgetting to update the moved value's index in the map leaves it pointing at a stale slot.
Removing the last element itself: i is the last index, so writing it onto itself and popping must still work (update the map before deleting val).
Returning a value from a separate HashSet for GetRandom is not O(1), and new Random() on every call can repeat values; create one Random and reuse it.
confusableWith: LRU Cache also pairs a dictionary with a second structure (a linked list), but to keep recency order; here order is irrelevant, so an array and swap-with-last suffice.
A plain HashSet gives O(1) insert and remove but has no O(1) random pick.

complexity.note: Each insert, remove and getRandom is O(1) on average: a few hash map operations, an append or pop at the end of the list, and one indexed read. The list and the map each hold the n current values.
